newsitem.title: USA: Cocaine cartel bought Mexican protection - witness.
newsitem.headline: Cocaine cartel bought Mexican protection - witness.

text.p: Millions of dollars in bribes were paid to high-level Mexican prosecutors to protect Juan Garcia Abrego's massive drug-smuggling operation, a confidant of the reputed kingpin testified on Tuesday.

Bribes totalling $1.5 million a month were paid to Javier Coello Trejo, a deputy attorney general in charge of Mexico's anti-drug efforts, and two other prosecutors, said Carlos Resendez, a close friend of Garcia Abrego and a chief lieutenant in the Gulf Cartel.

"They would be paid for protection, to be able to work with the cocaine, so they would be able to turn the other way," Resendez told jurors in Garcia Abrego's drug-trafficking and money-laundering trial.

Once on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list, Garcia Abrego faces up to life in prison if convicted on 22 counts contained in a federal indictment. He was captured in January in Monterrey, Mexico, and flown to Houston for trial.

Garcia Abrego's Gulf cartel was allegedly one of the most powerful drug-smuggling operations in Mexico, at one time moving more than a third of the cocaine used in the United States as the shipping arm of Colombia's Cali cartel.

Resendez, the latest in a parade of convicted Gulf cartel insiders to testify against the man known as "El Patron" -- "The Boss" -- said Garcia Abrego was hounded by police in the years before his capture, because bribes had not been delivered to prosecutors.

Garcia Abrego was forced to go into hiding on ranches near Monterrey in northern Mexico, and in 1990 he fled briefly to Chicago after warrants were issued for his arrest, Resendez said. "They were after him. They had an arrest order for him, and the problem came because of the money, they were not seeing it," Resendez said through a translator.
Garcia Abrego, after returning to Monterrey in early 1991, learned that an intermediary had pocketed more than $10 million in bribes sent to Coello Trejo, Resendez said.

Resendez, a former policeman and rancher who described himself as a "good friend" of Garcia Abrego, said the reputed kingpin owned several ranches in Mexico where cocaine-laden planes from Colombia landed and from which drugs were ferried north toward the U.S.-Mexican border.
Garcia Abrego also owned several thoroughbred racehorses, worked out of an office building in Monterrey, and ran a transportation company and several other legitimate businesses, Resendez said.

The Mexican Attorney General's Office alleges Garcia Abrego ran businesses ranging from hotels and gambling halls to newspapers and construction firms, the El Financiero newspaper reported Sunday in Mexico City.

He also held billions of dollars in bank accounts and investments, according to a 50-page report prepared by the Attorney General's Office. Details of Garcia Abrego's financial holdings were expected to emerge in testimony later this week.
